title: THE PLANET THAT KEPT A SPECIES AS DREAMS
deck: For four hundred years the planet Eda has held eighty thousand refugees in one shared dream, and the habitat built to wake them loses its funding in six days. Illuminara has until then to learn what the sleepers actually promised.
shape: Six scenes across six days: an empty wake-hall, the promise played back, the first sleeper, the weave that made the fear, four days of questions, and a morning with a window in it.

scenes.title: Eighty Thousand Empty Beds
paragraphs: *Ferrow Landing, the wake-hall · six days before the funding lapses*

The wake-hall had been built for eighty thousand and held none. Beds ran in rows to the far wall under a lamp that was kept lit out of habit, each with its sheet folded, its small cup, its name on a card in a script nobody on the surface could read any more. A notice from the Reconstruction Fund hung on the doorframe.
Marit Oen, who directed the Landing, met Illuminara at the door with her hand already out, as if for a rail.

**Marit**  
Before anything else: I don't want the planet hurt. Three delegations have asked me whether you could. I told them I'd rather you didn't know.

**Illuminara**  
Nobody has asked me to hurt anything. Tell me what Eda does when you ask.

**Marit**  
It sends rain. Four hundred years ago my people came here with one ship's worth of fear, and Eda took in all eighty thousand and put them to sleep in a single dream so none would wake alone. Every book calls it mercy. I turned eleven and asked when they would wake. It sent rain. The Fund pays for this hall while there is a wake date. On the seventh day there isn't one.

**Illuminara**  
What reason does it give?

**Marit**  
That it is keeping a promise. My council calls it a beautiful prison, and I have never been able to decide that they're wrong.

**Illuminara**  
Has anyone asked it what the promise says?
Nine generations of petitions lay in a cabinet behind her, every one of them asking for a date.

**Marit**  
They ask for waking. Nobody has asked what it's keeping.

**Illuminara**  
Then I'll ask that first.
Marit took a card from the nearest bed and held it out. *Halun Oen*, it read, and under it, in a second hand, *first in*.

**Marit**  
My great-grandfather. They tell me he's the one it talks to most.

scenes.title: The Promise, Played Back
paragraphs: *Inside the dream · the first hour*

She went in by the front door, which Eda had left unlatched as a sign of manners, and found a city-sized room of shared light: terraces stepping down to a slow river, and on every terrace people sitting, walking, sleeping inside their sleep. Rain fell without wetting anything. It was the loveliest thing she had seen in a hundred years, and she held that thought up and looked at it: loveliness was exactly how a good cage would feel from inside.

**Eda**  
You came by the door. Most visitors try the roof.

**Illuminara**  
I don't know the house. I'd rather be shown it.

The rain thinned, and the light bent into a memory: a ship broken on a dark plain, eighty thousand hollowed people, and a woman at their head who lifted her hands and spoke while every voice behind her spoke with her.

**Eda**  
They asked for a quiet in which no hand could be raised. I have kept it for four hundred years. You will tell me they are free to choose now. They were free then. They used it to end a world. I am not a jailer, Illuminara. I am the promise they made when they still remembered the cost.

**Illuminara**  
I believe that. I think you have been faithful for four hundred years to something nobody was ever allowed to check. Will you play me the last clause again? Only that.

**Eda**  
No. You want to read it as a door, and everyone who has read it as a door has stood in it. If I ask and they say wake, and I am wrong about the danger, I will have spent them on a question. I would rather be called a jailer for four hundred years than be the one who asked.

**Illuminara**  
Then I won't ask them anything you haven't heard first. Nothing leaves your weave without your hand on it, and I'll never ask you for a date. Only for the clause, here, with you holding it.
The woman lifted her hands. *Keep us from ourselves,* said eighty thousand voices, *until we can bear to be asked.*

**Illuminara**  
Who decides when that has happened?

**Eda**  
I do. They gave me the judgment. I have weighed their bearing against the world they left, and it has never been safe enough.

**Illuminara**  
But the clause doesn't end when the world is safe. It ends when they can bear to be asked. Who can tell you that, without being asked?
The rain stopped. It stopped like a person who halts mid-stride, not like a tap being shut.

**Eda**  
I am asked for dates, rights, harbours, cures, weather. I have never been asked what I am afraid of, and I have never asked them anything, because the promise was made by all of them at once and a promise cannot ask.

**Illuminara**  
What are you afraid of?

**Eda**  
Come and meet Halun. Then ask me again.

scenes.title: What Safe Would Look Like
paragraphs: *Inside the dream · beside the river*

Halun Oen was fishing in a river that held no fish. He was very old and lucid in the way of a man who has had four centuries to rehearse his thoughts, and he looked at her with the pleasure of someone who has not been surprised in a long while.

**Halun**  
You're the visitor. Eda says you came by the door.

**Illuminara**  
I'm not selling anything, and I'm not here to open anyone's eyes. What would have to be true before you felt safe?

**Halun**  
Nobody has asked me that since the ship. Eda asks whether I'm comfortable. I am. That's a different question, and it has been answering for the first one for a very long time. Safe would be this: no one can arrive at my door with a reason; I can say no to a person I love and not be punished by their face; and my granddaughter's grandchildren are fed, because I can't see them and I find I mind.

**Illuminara**  
One of them is standing in the wake-hall. She's wearing the look of someone who has prepared a speech.
Halun laughed, a dry startled sound that carried down the terraces, and several sleepers turned in their sleep toward it.

**Halun**  
Is she wearing a coat?

**Illuminara**  
A grey one, buttoned wrong.

**Halun**  
Then she's mine. Listen, visitor. Whatever you do, don't ask me for the others. I know about me. I don't know whether I'd leave. I would like to be allowed not to know for a few days.
Illuminara found, a little to her own surprise, that she had put one hand flat against her chest, as if to keep something from spilling.

scenes.title: The Weave
paragraphs: *Inside the dream · the terrace above the river, that night*

**Illuminara**  
Now I'll ask it again. What are you afraid of?

Eda showed her, and it was not a speech. It was a terrace very like this one, fifty-one years ago, and a young man called Sefa Dunn whom a visiting delegation had begged Eda to let go. Eda had let him go. The dream was woven so that each sleeper's pattern held the pattern beside it, and when Sefa's thread was drawn out the tear ran through the whole weave. Nine hundred sleepers seized. Three did not come back.

**Eda**  
I did not refuse them out of principle. I refused because I felt it. Three. I have their names.

**Illuminara**  
Thank you for showing me. That's a better reason than the one you gave in the hall.

She sat on the terrace wall and thought about the weave as she had once thought about a collapsing corridor: as a load path, not a moral. Sefa had left through the shared dream. The tear ran through everything because everything was holding hands.

**Illuminara**  
It's the exit that kills them, not the waking. What if nobody leaves through the shared dream? What if each sleeper is first moved into a room of their own, a stitched pocket, and wakes from there? The tear would end at the pocket's wall.

**Eda**  
A wall. The promise had no walls.

**Illuminara**  
A pocket with a window, then. They could still see one another, and change their minds in either direction.
For a long time there was only the river.

**Illuminara**  
Do you know how to build it?

**Eda**  
Better than you. I wove the thing. The seam you'd sew would tear. I'd lay it as a breath lays, in and then out, so the neighbours barely feel the stitch. But I cannot hold the surrounding weave steady and sew at the same moment. I never needed a second pair of hands.

Illuminara put both palms to the air as if to the side of a very large animal and felt the whole weave lean on her: eighty thousand patterns, each somebody's single life. She was strong enough. That was the one thing she was certain of, and it was not what she had come to use.

**Illuminara**  
Sew. I'll keep it still.

Eda chose a woman at the edge of the third terrace and began. The pocket closed round her like folded water, a window opened in its wall, and her pattern, quiet for four centuries, leaned toward the pattern of the sleeper beyond the glass, as a plant leans to a lit pane. Along the seam the dream gave its first small shiver.

**Eda**  
It's tearing.
Illuminara did not push against the lean. She held the weave around it and looked at what the window showed: a neighbour's raw thread, and a thread pulls at any thread it can see.

**Illuminara**  
Stop. It's the window. It shows her the wiring. Someone looking out of a window sees a face and the weather. Show her what a hand would see through glass.

**Eda**  
Light, then, and a shape that can wave. Not the thread.

Eda unpicked the stitch a breath at a time while Illuminara held the lean until it went slack. The second window showed a hand-sized square of afternoon and the outline of a neighbour sitting up, and the woman's pattern did not lean at all. Illuminara kept the weave still for eleven minutes while the light closed round her, and the dream did not so much as tremble. When the pocket held she could not speak for an hour. Eda was kind enough not to ask her to.

scenes.title: Four Days of Questions
paragraphs: *Inside the dream · the second to the fifth day*

Eda could hold eighty thousand conversations at once, and had never held one. It split itself into pockets and asked each sleeper the same three sentences: *You are safe in a room of your own. You may wake into the habitat, stay in the dream, or say you do not know yet. Whatever you say, I will ask you again, and I will not take it as a vote that binds anyone else.*

Illuminara sat on the terrace through the nights, holding the weave still while the pockets were laid, and the first answers came as weather. Warm rains, a thousand of them. One hard hail from a man who wanted to hear what the reconstruction did with the ones who stayed. A child's sleeping laugh nobody had interpreted in four centuries, which turned out to mean *yes, please*.

**Eda**  
I did not expect so many to say yes, or so many to say no. One question, eighty thousand different weathers.

**Illuminara**  
How many?

**Eda**  
Sixty-one thousand two hundred and four will wake. Eighteen thousand seven hundred and ninety-six will stay, or will say not yet.
Eda's voice had a grain in it now. Illuminara knew it from her own long memory, from counting how many of the people she had loved had chosen to go.

**Eda**  
It will be a quieter world.

**Illuminara**  
It will. I won't say it won't. I'll tell you who is going to ask you the next question, because I think you've been alone in this house a very long time.

**Eda**  
No one has ever asked me.

**Illuminara**  
Every six months the ones who stay are asked again, in their pockets, in their own words. And they may ask you: what are you afraid of now? That's the promise made to hold. Not their silence. Their answer, given again.
The rain began, very softly, and for the first time it was wet.

scenes.title: A Window in the Hall
paragraphs: *Ferrow Landing, the wake-hall · the sixth day, morning*

The first cohort came out of the pockets one bed at a time in the long light of the wake-hall, while the Fund's auditors recorded nothing worse than coughing. A girl called Iri Kesh, nineteen and a little affronted, set her feet on a floor for the first time in four hundred years, looked at the lamp that had been kept lit for her, and said she would like to know who had been paying for the electricity.

The auditors signed the extension at nine: the hall for a year, the rest of the waking in cohorts of two thousand. The housing board had begun its quarrel about what a person owns who has slept twelve generations; four hundred families on the surface had discovered they were someone's descendants and did not know what to do with their hands. The ones who stayed lay on in their pockets by their own choice, and Marit's council could not agree whether to call that a victory.
Marit had spent the morning walking the rows with a box of name-cards, reading each name aloud before she set the card back on its bed. She had learned to say the names.

Halun had stayed. He had told Eda so on the fourth day, kindly, and asked one condition, which Eda built before nightfall: a glass in the wake-hall wall, a hand's breadth across, that looked into his pocket from outside and out from his pocket in.
Marit stood in front of it in her grey coat, buttoned wrong. She had her speech. She did not give it.

**Halun**  
Is she wearing a coat?

**Marit**  
I'm wearing a coat, Grandfather.

**Halun**  
Good. It's raining up there, isn't it. Come closer. I haven't seen the weather from the wrong side in four hundred years.

**Marit**  
The council still calls this a prison. This morning I told them a prison is a place where nobody asks, and this one has been asking all week.

**Halun**  
And?

**Marit**  
They didn't like it. I'm going to keep saying it.

Marit laid her palm on the glass. On the far side an old man lifted his own to meet it, and in the dream behind him a river ran with the first fish it had ever held, and the rain fell and was wet on both of them.

Illuminara stood in the doorway as long as she could, which was not long: there were people still to be asked in six months and more still to be woken, and she was tired in the way of someone who has set down a heavy thing and has not yet been told to leave it there. Eda's voice reached her once more through the lamp over the door, no louder than a weather report.

**Eda**  
Come back and be asked.

**Illuminara**  
I will. It's your turn.

critic_line: A planet that kept a promise nobody was allowed to check learns to be asked, through a window Illuminara redesigned and a seam Eda chose to sew.
